newsitem.title: USA: Turnover in top USDA offices likely - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Turnover in top USDA offices likely - analysts.

text.p: Election Day could be the equivalent of the neutron bomb for political appointees at the U.S. Agriculture Department -- creating vacancies for several key jobs even if President Clinton is re-elected.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman was likely to remain as head of the department, analysts said Monday. Glickman has repeatedly said he enjoys the cabinet post.

However, analysts said it was likely Undersecretary Gene Moos and Deputy Secretary Richard Rominger would not stay for a second term. Moos has noted he soon will turn 72. Rominger unsuccessfully sought Glickman's job two years ago.

There also was speculation that two undersecretaries who have been criticized on Capitol Hill, James Lyons and Ellen Haas, may depart. Haas oversees nutrition programs and Lyons is in charge of soil conservation and national forests.

By one gauge, the turnover already has begun. Michael Taylor, undersecretary for food safety, has said he will leave in mid-November and Jack Ward Thomas has announced his retirement as Forest Service chief.

"It could be a fairly clean sweep (of sub-cabinet posts)," said private consultant John Schnittker. If there was a large turnover, he said, it could take months to select successors and win Senate confirmation.
A Glickman spokesman declined to comment on who might leave the department.
"I don't imagine we'll be commenting on personnel matters at this juncture," said spokesman Jim Petterson.

One analyst, who asked not to be named, said the election, a traditional point for job changes, might lead to the departure of Grant Buntrock, head of the Farm Service Agency. He has denied any wrongdoing but was accused at a House hearing of violating rules against political activity at work.

New leadership was certain for the House Agricutlure Committee. Chairman Pat Roberts, Kansas Republican, was running for the Senate and the panel's Democratic leader, Kike de la Garza of Texas, will retire.

House Republican leaders have indicated Bob Smith of Oregon would succeed Roberts in seniority. Texan Charles Stenholm was widely expected to be the top Democrat. Depending on which party controls the House, Smith or Stenholm would be chairman and the other would be minority leader on the panel.

Analysts said the decade-long leadership team of Vermont Democrat Pat Leahy and Indiana Republican Richard Lugar on the Senate Agriculture Committee might be splintered. They painted scenarios in which Leahy might become Judiciary chairman or Lugar switch to another committee.

Leahy aides declined to comment on the rumors. A spokesman for Lugar, now the Agriculture chairman, said that conditions favored continued Republican control of the Senate and re-election of incumbents, which would mean "line-ups will remain exactly as we have."
